name: Title with a Personal Name

1.definition: Uses a personal name and a convention for identifying the bearer’s office, qualification, or style.
1.details: The title helps determine the form of the associated name. In the conventional British uses illustrated here, Sir precedes a given name, with a surname optionally following. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style. Some professional conventions and familiar styles use a title with a given name.

projection.target: Substituting a surname alone for the given name in the standard British Sir pattern loses the conventional name form. A professional title such as Dr can use the surname alone.
projection.evidence: CASA distinguishes academic title plus surname from title plus given name. CGEL gives examples of both as possible personal names in vocative function.

curious.title: Titles that go with names
curious.summary: A title such as Sir or Dr can sit in front of a person's name, and the title helps decide which form of the name follows.
curious.body: In Sir James opened the ceremony, the title Sir goes with a given name. In Dr Patel wrote the report, the title Dr goes with a surname. The title tells us something about the person, such as an office or a qualification, and it also shapes the name that comes after it. The dictionary describes this as a convention, and marks its account as provisional. In the conventional British uses covered here, Sir precedes a given name, and a surname may follow it. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style. Some professional conventions and familiar styles use a title with a given name.
curious.try: Think of a title you know, such as Dr or Sir. Which kind of name do you put after it, a first name or a surname?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining which part of a person's name follows a title such as Sir or Dr.
teacher.explain: A title is a pre-head element in a noun phrase whose head is a personal name, and the title is tied to a conventional name form. In the conventional British uses this dictionary illustrates, Sir precedes a given name, with a surname optionally following. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style, though some professional conventions and familiar styles pair a title with a given name. This dictionary says that replacing the given name with a surname alone in the standard Sir pattern loses the conventional name form, while a professional title such as Dr can use the surname alone. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, so present these as conventions, not rules for every variety.
teacher.terms: Title is the traditional name for Sir and Dr in this use. This dictionary treats the whole sequence as a noun phrase with a personal name.
watch_for: A learner might assume the same part of the name follows every title.
A learner might use a surname alone after Sir, though this dictionary says this loses the conventional name form.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of titles and a list of people's names. In pairs they match each title with the name forms the conventions allow, then compare with the teacher's list.
